claim: Clec9A is a C-type lectin-like receptor critical for recognition and processing of dead cells.
source: The C-type lectin-like receptor Clec9A (also known as DNGR1) is critical for recognition and processing of dead cells, and is a key defining marker of the cDC1 subset (Ahrens et al., 2012; Caminschi et al., 2008; Huysamen et al., 2008; Sancho et al., 2009; Sancho et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: Clec9A is a key defining marker of the cDC1 subset.
source: The C-type lectin-like receptor Clec9A (also known as DNGR1) is critical for recognition and processing of dead cells, and is a key defining marker of the cDC1 subset (Ahrens et al., 2012; Caminschi et al., 2008; Huysamen et al., 2008; Sancho et al., 2009; Sancho et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: Clec9A recognizes dead cells once their cell membrane is disrupted, exposing internal cellular components.
source: Clec9A recognizes dead cells once their cell membrane is disrupted, exposing internal cellular components (Ahrens et al., 2012; Sancho et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: The Clec9A ligand exposed upon cell death is the filamentous form of actin (F-actin).
source: The Clec9A ligand exposed upon cell death is the filamentous form of actin (F-actin), which is normally associated with actin-binding proteins (Ahrens et al., 2012; Schulz et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2012) and potentially with Ag from within the dead cell.
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Clec9A directs material to early and recycling endosomes, favoring Ag processing and presentation, rather than to phagolysosomes for degradation.
source: Clec9A directs material to early and recycling endosomes, favoring Ag processing and presentation, rather than to phagolysosomes for degradation (Zelenay et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: cDC1 from Clec9A knockout mice have a reduced capacity for cross-presentation of dead cell-derived Ag.
source: cDC1 from Clec9A knockout mice have a reduced capacity for cross-presentation of dead cell-derived Ag (Sancho et al., 2009) and are more susceptible to viral infection (Zelenay et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: cDC1 from Clec9A knockout mice are more susceptible to viral infection.
source: cDC1 from Clec9A knockout mice have a reduced capacity for cross-presentation of dead cell-derived Ag (Sancho et al., 2009) and are more susceptible to viral infection (Zelenay et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Delivering Ag to cDC1 using monoclonal antibodies against Clec9A has proved very effective in enhancing immune responses and improving vaccine efficacies.
source: Consistent with the role of Clec9A in enhancing immunity, delivering Ag to cDC1 using monoclonal antibodies against Clec9A, has proved very effective in enhancing immune responses and improving vaccine efficacies (Caminschi et al., 2008; Lahoud et al., 2011; Sancho et al., 2008; Tullett et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Targeting Clec9A enhances CD8+ T cell responses and cytotoxic T cell generation.
source: Targeting Clec9A not only enhances CD8+ T cell responses and cytotoxic T cell generation (Caminschi et al., 2008; Sancho et al., 2008), but surprisingly also promotes CD4+ T cell responses, as supported by the role of cDC1 in promoting both CD8+ and CD4+ T cell responses (Ferris et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Targeting Clec9A promotes CD4+ T cell responses.
source: Targeting Clec9A not only enhances CD8+ T cell responses and cytotoxic T cell generation (Caminschi et al., 2008; Sancho et al., 2008), but surprisingly also promotes CD4+ T cell responses, as supported by the role of cDC1 in promoting both CD8+ and CD4+ T cell responses (Ferris et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Targeting Clec9A primes follicular helper T cells and induces potent humoral responses even in the absence of adjuvants.
source: Indeed, targeting Clec9A primes follicular helper T cells and induces potent humoral responses even in the absence of adjuvants (Caminschi et al., 2008; Lahoud et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: RNF41 is a member of the RING family widely expressed in immune cells.
source: RNF41, a member of the RING family widely expressed in immune cells, directly binds and ubiquitinates target proteins, targeting them for downstream fates such as proteasomal degradation (e.g. ErbB3, MyD88, USP8) or to regulate protein trafficking (VPS52) (Bouyain and Leahy, 2007; De Ceuninck et al., 2013; Masschaele et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: RNF41 directly binds and ubiquitinates target proteins, targeting them for downstream fates such as proteasomal degradation or to regulate protein trafficking.
source: RNF41, a member of the RING family widely expressed in immune cells, directly binds and ubiquitinates target proteins, targeting them for downstream fates such as proteasomal degradation (e.g. ErbB3, MyD88, USP8) or to regulate protein trafficking (VPS52) (Bouyain and Leahy, 2007; De Ceuninck et al., 2013; Masschaele et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: RNF41 modulates immune responses through Toll-like receptor pathways by ubiquitinating MyD88 and the kinase TBK1.
source: RNF41 also modulates immune responses through Toll-like receptor pathways by ubiquitinating MyD88 and the kinase TBK1 (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: RNF41 regulates the sorting of endosomal proteins by ubiquitinating Ubiquitin-Specific Protease 8 (USP8).
source: In addition, RNF41 regulates the sorting of endosomal proteins by ubiquitinating Ubiquitin-Specific Protease 8 (USP8), which in turn regulates the stability of the Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport (ESCRT)−0 protein complex (De Ceuninck et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Mouse Clec9A ectodomain bound to human RNF41 on protein microarrays.
source: We found mClec9A-ecto bound to human RNF41, whereas an independent control C-type lectin, Cire/DC-SIGN, did not bind RNF41 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Experimental data from protein microarray experiments

claim: mClec9A-ecto did not bind to 29 other members of the RNF family present on the arrays.
source: In addition, mClec9A-ecto did not bind to 29 other members of the RNF family present on the arrays, indicating a specific interaction between Clec9A and RNF41.
evidence: Experimental data from protein microarray experiments

claim: The interaction between Clec9A and RNF41 is specific.
source: In addition, mClec9A-ecto did not bind to 29 other members of the RNF family present on the arrays, indicating a specific interaction between Clec9A and RNF41.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing lack of binding to other RNF family members

claim: Human and mouse RNF41 differ by only one amino acid.
source: The E3 ubiquitin ligase RNF41 is highly conserved across species, with only one amino acid difference between human and mouse RNF41.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of protein sequences

claim: mClec9A-ecto directly bound to RNF41, but not to control GST protein.
source: We found that mClec9A-ecto directly bound to RNF41, but not to control GST protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in figure supplement

claim: Control C-type lectin ectodomain, Clec12A-ecto did not bind to RNF41.
source: By contrast, independent control C-type lectin ectodomain, Clec12A-ecto (Zhang et al., 2012) did not bind to RNF41 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in figure supplement

claim: mClec9A-ecto bound the C-terminal domain of RNF41 (RNF41-C), but not the N-terminal domains (RNF41-RBC).
source: mClec9A-ecto bound the C-terminal domain of RNF41 (RNF41-C), but not the N-terminal domains (RNF41-RBC) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in figure supplement

claim: Both mClec9A-ecto and hCLEC9A-ecto bound to RNF41 C-terminal domains, but not to N-terminal domains or GST controls.
source: This was confirmed using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA); both mClec9A-ecto and hCLEC9A-ecto bound to RNF41 C-terminal domains, but not to N-terminal domains or GST controls, whereas the control mClec12A-ecto showed no binding to any of the RNF41 constructs (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Experimental data from ELISA shown in figures

claim: The Clec9A-RNF41 interaction is conserved in humans and mice.
source: This confirmed that Clec9A binds specifically to the RNF41 C-terminal domain and that the Clec9A-RNF41 interaction is conserved in humans and mice.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing both mouse and human Clec9A bind RNF41

claim: Clec9A recognition of dead cells via binding to F-actin requires conserved tryptophan residues located in the Clec9A-CTLD (hCLEC9A W131 and W227; mClec9A W155 and W250).
source: Clec9A recognition of dead cells via binding to its ligand F-actin, requires conserved tryptophan residues located in the Clec9A-CTLD (hCLEC9A W131 and W227; mClec9A W155 and W250) (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Wild-type and mutated hCLEC9A (W131A, W227A) bound comparably to RNF41.
source: Wild-type and mutated hCLEC9A (W131A, W227A) bound comparably to RNF41, indicating that the Clec9A residues required for binding F-actin differed from those required for binding RNF41 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in figure supplement

claim: The Clec9A residues required for binding F-actin differ from those required for binding RNF41.
source: Wild-type and mutated hCLEC9A (W131A, W227A) bound comparably to RNF41, indicating that the Clec9A residues required for binding F-actin differed from those required for binding RNF41 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing mutant Clec9A still binds RNF41

claim: RNF41 bound to Clec9A comparably both in the presence or absence of actin.
source: RNF41 bound to Clec9A comparably both in the presence or absence of actin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F) indicating that actin and RNF41 do not compete for Clec9A binding.
evidence: Experimental data shown in figure supplement

claim: Actin and RNF41 do not compete for Clec9A binding.
source: RNF41 bound to Clec9A comparably both in the presence or absence of actin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F) indicating that actin and RNF41 do not compete for Clec9A binding.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing no competition

claim: Pre-incubation of Clec9A with 10B4 partially inhibited Clec9A-RNF41 binding.
source: Pre-incubation of Clec9A with 10B4 partially inhibited Clec9A-RNF41 binding, suggesting that Clec9A binding to RNF41 was mediated, at least in part, via the Clec9A CTLD long loop region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Experimental data shown in figure supplement

claim: Clec9A binding to RNF41 is mediated, at least in part, via the Clec9A CTLD long loop region.
source: Pre-incubation of Clec9A with 10B4 partially inhibited Clec9A-RNF41 binding, suggesting that Clec9A binding to RNF41 was mediated, at least in part, via the Clec9A CTLD long loop region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Inferred from antibody inhibition experiment

claim: Clec9A exists as a disulfide-bonded homodimer, which can adopt either a reversible reduction-sensitive (type-1) or a reduction-resistant (type-2) dimer conformation.
source: Clec9A exists as a disulfide-bonded homodimer, which can adopt either a reversible reduction-sensitive (type-1) or a reduction-resistant (type-2) dimer conformation (Hanč et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: At lower pH, both mouse and human Clec9A adopt a reduction-resistant dimer conformation.
source: At lower pH, both mouse and human Clec9A adopt a reduction-resistant dimer conformation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from cited research

claim: The reduction-resistant conformation of Clec9A promotes cross-presentation of dead cell-derived Ag.
source: This reduction-resistant conformation promotes cross-presentation of dead cell-derived Ag, although it does not affect the ability of Clec9A to bind its ligand F-actin, to signal through Syk kinase or to undergo internalization (Hanč et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Clec9A binding to RNF41 was potentiated at lower pH.
source: We observed that Clec9A binding to RNF41 was potentiated at lower pH (Figure 1C,D), suggesting that the enhanced binding of the reduction-resistant Clec9A dimer, such as found in low pH endosomes, to RNF41, may play a role in cross-presentation.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D

claim: The enhanced binding of the reduction-resistant Clec9A dimer to RNF41 may play a role in cross-presentation.
source: We observed that Clec9A binding to RNF41 was potentiated at lower pH (Figure 1C,D), suggesting that the enhanced binding of the reduction-resistant Clec9A dimer, such as found in low pH endosomes, to RNF41, may play a role in cross-presentation.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental data

claim: RNF41 has a putative-N-terminal myristoylation site, thought to anchor RNF41 to intracellular membranes.
source: RNF41 has a putative-N-terminal myristoylation site, thought to anchor RNF41 to intracellular membranes (Masschaele et al., 2017; Masschaele et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: The major RNF41 isoform (~39 kDa) is primarily associated with digitonin soluble fractions containing cytosol and early endosomes in cDC1.
source: Cellular fractionation studies of cDC1 indicated the major RNF41 isoform (~39 kDa) was primarily associated with digitonin soluble fractions containing cytosol and early endosomes (indicated by GAPDH and EEA-1 expression), but was also associated with detergent (IGEPAL)-resistant membrane fractions (Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental data from cellular fractionation shown in Figure 2A

claim: A larger RNF41 isoform (~55 kDa) is differentially associated with IGEPAL soluble membrane fractions, including endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and recycling endosomes.
source: We also observed a larger RNF41 isoform (~55 kDa) that was differentially associated with IGEPAL soluble membrane fractions, including endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and recycling endosomes (indicated by Calreticulin and Rab11 expression).
evidence: Experimental data from cellular fractionation

claim: Clec9A is found in Digitonin soluble fractions containing early endosomes, in IGEPAL soluble fractions containing recycling endosomes and in detergent-resistant membrane fractions.
source: Consistent with its role as an endocytic membrane receptor, Clec9A was found in Digitonin soluble fractions containing early endosomes, in IGEPAL soluble fractions containing recycling endosomes and in detergent-resistant membrane fractions.
evidence: Experimental data from cellular fractionation

claim: RNF41 is expressed both in the cytoplasm and associated with endosomal vesicles in cDC1.
source: Microscopy studies of cDC1 confirmed RNF41 expression both in the cytoplasm and associated with endosomal vesicles, as indicated by colocalization with EEA-1 and Rab11, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Experimental data from microscopy shown in figure supplement

claim: RNF41 localizes to the cytoplasm, the plasma membrane and intracellular membranes such as ER, early endosomes, late endosomes, endosomal tubular-vesicular compartments.
source: We further demonstrated localization of RNF41 to the cytoplasm, the plasma membrane and intracellular membranes such as ER, early endosomes, late endosomes, endosomal tubular-vesicular compartments, based on the morphological characteristics of these compartments using immuno-electron microscopy (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental data from immuno-electron microscopy shown in figure supplement

claim: Clec9A and RNF41 can be found in similar types of membrane-associated intracellular compartments.
source: Thus, our data indicate that Clec9A and RNF41 can be found in similar types of membrane-associated intracellular compartments.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing colocalization

claim: RNF41 and the extracellular domain of Clec9A colocalize within 40 nm in cDC1.
source: RNF41 and the extracellular domain of Clec9A colocalized within 40 nm in cDC1, indicative of an in situ Clec9A-RNF41 interaction within DC (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental data from proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 2B

claim: Treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 enhanced Clec9A and RNF41 interactions within steady-state cDC1.
source: Treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 enhanced Clec9A and RNF41 interactions within steady-state cDC1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A: No dead cells), suggesting that one outcome of the Clec9A-RNF41 interaction may be for RNF41 to ubiquitinate and target Clec9A, or its associated Ag cargo, for proteasomal degradation.
evidence: Experimental data shown in figure supplement

claim: One outcome of the Clec9A-RNF41 interaction may be for RNF41 to ubiquitinate and target Clec9A, or its associated Ag cargo, for proteasomal degradation.
source: Treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 enhanced Clec9A and RNF41 interactions within steady-state cDC1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A: No dead cells), suggesting that one outcome of the Clec9A-RNF41 interaction may be for RNF41 to ubiquitinate and target Clec9A, or its associated Ag cargo, for proteasomal degradation.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental data with proteasome inhibitor

claim: Knockdown of RNF41 in cDC1 using shRNA#5 resulted in significantly enhanced cross-presentation of dead cell-associated Ag.
source: Knockdown of RNF41 in cDC1 using shRNA#5 resulted in significantly enhanced cross-presentation of dead cell-associated Ag (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), whereas the modest reduction of RNF41 using shRNA #10 only resulted in a slight enhancement of cross-presentation that did not reach statistical significance (Figure 2D).
evidence: Experimental data from T cell proliferation assays shown in figures

claim: Knockdown of RNF41 resulted in enhanced MHC II presentation of dead cell-derived Ag.
source: Similarly, knockdown of RNF41 resulted in enhanced MHC II presentation of dead cell-derived Ag (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), albeit the absolute level of CD4 T cell stimulation by cDC1 was lower than that of CD8 T cells, as expected for cDC1 (Rizzitelli et al., 2006).
evidence: Experimental data from T cell proliferation assays shown in figures

claim: RNF41 down-regulates the processing of dead cell-associated Ag for both MHC II presentation and MHC I cross-presentation.
source: This data suggested that RNF41 down-regulates the processing of dead cell-associated Ag for both MHC II presentation and MHC I cross-presentation.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing enhanced presentation with RNF41 knockdown

claim: Co-transfection of RNF41 and Clec9A resulted in reduced Clec9A levels, both at the level of total cellular expression and at the cell surface.
source: Co-transfection of RNF41 and Clec9A resulted in reduced Clec9A levels, both at the level of total cellular expression and at the cell surface (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Experimental data from transfection experiments shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: Co-expression of a control E3 ubiquitin ligase RNF6 did not affect Clec9A levels.
source: By contrast, co-expression of a control E3 ubiquitin ligase RNF6 did not affect Clec9A levels (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Experimental data from transfection experiments shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: RNF41 regulation of both mouse and human Clec9A levels was dependent on the RING domain that is necessary for ubiquitin transfer.
source: RNF41 regulation of both mouse and human Clec9A levels was dependent on the RING domain that is necessary for ubiquitin transfer, as expression of full-length RNF41 resulted in reduced Clec9A levels, whereas the truncated RNF41 (RNF41-ΔRING) that lacks the RING domain, had no effects on Clec9A levels (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Experimental data from transfection experiments shown in Figure 3C,D

claim: RNF41 did not regulate levels of control receptor Clec12A.
source: RNF41 did not regulate levels of control receptor Clec12A, confirming specificity of RNF41 regulation of Clec9A (Figure 3C).
evidence: Experimental data from transfection experiments shown in Figure 3C

claim: RNF41-mediated ubiquitination of Clec9A promotes its degradation.
source: Overall, this suggests that RNF41-mediated ubiquitination of Clec9A promotes its degradation, most likely at the ER or endosomal compartments, and that this restrains Ag presentation.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing reduced Clec9A levels with RNF41

claim: Co-transfection of RNF41 with a recombinant form of Clec9A, which includes extracellular domains but lacks transmembrane and intracellular domains (Clec9A-ecto), resulted in reduced Clec9A-ecto levels.
source: Co-transfection of RNF41 with a recombinant form of Clec9A, which includes extracellular domains but lacks transmembrane and intracellular domains (Clec9A-ecto), resulted in reduced Clec9A-ecto levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental data shown in figure supplement

claim: RNF41 interaction with the extracellular domains of Clec9A is sufficient to regulate Clec9A fate.
source: This suggested that RNF41 interaction with the extracellular domains of Clec9A is sufficient to regulate Clec9A fate.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing regulation of Clec9A-ecto

claim: It is the co-expression of Clec9A and RNF41 within the same cell that facilitates RNF41 regulation of Clec9A.
source: We further excluded the possibility that Clec9A might interact with RNF41 released from damaged or neighboring cells, indicating that it is the co-expression of Clec9A and RNF41 within the same cell that facilitates RNF41 regulation of Clec9A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Experimental data from mixing experiments shown in figure supplement

claim: Two forms of the Clec9A dimer were identified: a ~ 75 kDa mature protein with post ER-glycosylation, and a ~ 60 kDa form with less complex, high mannose, glycosylation indicative of a newly synthesized protein.
source: Using western blot analysis under non-reducing conditions and Liquid Chromatography Tandem Mass-Spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), we identified two forms of the Clec9A dimer: a ~ 75 kDa mature protein with post ER-glycosylation, and a ~ 60 kDa form with less complex, high mannose, glycosylation indicative of a newly synthesized protein (Figure 3E, Supplementary file 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental data from western blot and mass spectrometry

claim: Brefeldin A treatment resulted in a reduction of the mature Clec9A dimer, and an increase in the newly synthesized Clec9A dimer.
source: To determine whether RNF41 acts on Clec9A at the ER, we used Brefeldin A to inhibit transport of newly synthesized proteins from the ER/Golgi to the cell surface. This resulted in a reduction of the mature Clec9A dimer, and an increase in the newly synthesized Clec9A dimer (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Experimental data from Brefeldin A treatment shown in figures

claim: Brefeldin A did not inhibit RNF41-mediated degradation of Clec9A.
source: However, Brefeldin A did not inhibit RNF41-mediated degradation of Clec9A (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Experimental data from Brefeldin A treatment shown in figures

claim: Co-expression of Clec9A with RNF41, in the presence of Brefeldin A, resulted in reduced levels of the newly synthesized ER-resident form of Clec9A.
source: Moreover, co-expression of Clec9A with RNF41, in the presence of Brefeldin A, resulted in reduced levels of the newly synthesized ER-resident form of Clec9A (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Experimental data from Brefeldin A treatment shown in figures

claim: RNF41 can regulate levels of newly synthesized Clec9A at the ER.
source: These data demonstrate that as well as potentially interacting in endosomal compartments (Figure 2—figure supplements 1E and 2), RNF41 can also regulate levels of newly synthesized Clec9A at the ER.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data with Brefeldin A

claim: In the presence of full-length RNF41, there was a 4-fold or greater increase in the abundance of 17 Clec9A-interacting proteins.
source: However, in the presence of full-length RNF41, we observed a 4-fold or greater increase in the abundance of 17 Clec9A-interacting proteins, considering a false discovery rate (FDR) cutoff of 0.05 (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Experimental data from proteomic analysis shown in figures

claim: An increased association of Clec9A with ER membrane protein Erlin2 (4-fold), ER chaperones calreticulin (CALR >4 fold) and calnexin (CANX >2 fold), and with translocon Sec61A1 (>3.5 fold) was identified.
source: Focusing on ER-associated proteins, we identified an increased association of Clec9A with ER membrane protein Erlin2 (4-fold), ER chaperones calreticulin (CALR >4 fold) and calnexin (CANX >2 fold), and with translocon Sec61A1 (>3.5 fold), supporting a role for RNF41 in ER-associated regulation of Clec9A in steady state.
evidence: Experimental data from proteomic analysis

claim: Most Clec9A-interactions, including Erlin2 and Calreticulin, may be enhanced by ubiquitination mediated by the RING domain, rather than RNF41 binding per se.
source: Comparison of Clec9A-interacting proteins in the presence of RNF41 versus RNF41-Δ RING indicated that most of these Clec9A-interactions, including Erlin2 and Calreticulin, may be enhanced by ubiquitination mediated by the RING domain, rather than RNF41 binding per se (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Experimental data from proteomic analysis shown in figure supplement

claim: There was an increased Clec9A interaction with proteasomal complex component PSMB1.
source: It further revealed an increased Clec9A interaction with proteasomal complex component PSMB1, confirming RNF41-mediated regulation of Clec9A can be associated with proteasomal degradation.
evidence: Experimental data from proteomic analysis

claim: Erlin1 and Erlin2 are highly expressed by cDC1.
source: We initially focused on the ER-associated proteins Erlin2 and Erlin1 (Browman et al., 2006), identified as potentially interacting with Clec9A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G), as they are highly expressed by cDC1 (Theisen et al., 2018) and have been shown to facilitate recruitment of E3 ubiquitin ligases to receptors (Lu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Erlin1 and Erlin2 have been shown to facilitate recruitment of E3 ubiquitin ligases to receptors.
source: We initially focused on the ER-associated proteins Erlin2 and Erlin1 (Browman et al., 2006), identified as potentially interacting with Clec9A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G), as they are highly expressed by cDC1 (Theisen et al., 2018) and have been shown to facilitate recruitment of E3 ubiquitin ligases to receptors (Lu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Clec9A interacts with endogenous Erlin1 and Erlin2.
source: We validated the novel Clec9A interaction with endogenous Erlin1 and Erlin2 by co-IP studies of Clec9A transfected 293 F cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: Experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation shown in figure supplement

claim: The Clec9A-Erlin1/2 interactions were increased in the presence of RNF41 in a RING domain-dependent manner.
source: We further demonstrated that the Clec9A-Erlin1/2 interactions were increased in the presence of RNF41 in a RING domain-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J), although the total levels of endogenous Erlin1 and Erlin2 did not change (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I: Input samples).
evidence: Experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation shown in figure supplement

claim: The Clec9A-Erlin 1/2 interaction is associated with RNF41 regulation of Clec9A.
source: Given that the RNF41 RING domain is required for RNF41-mediated regulation of Clec9A, these data favor a model in which the Clec9A-Erlin 1/2 interaction is associated with RNF41 regulation of Clec9A.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing RING domain dependence

claim: RNF41 mediated poly-ubiquitination of mClec9A and hCLEC9A.
source: As expected, RNF41 mediated poly-ubiquitination of mClec9A and hCLEC9A, whereas RNF41-ΔRING did not mediate increased ubiquitination of Clec9A above the levels observed by transfection with Clec9A alone (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Experimental data from ubiquitination assays shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: Purified RNF41 was able to mediate ubiquitination of Clec9A in vitro.
source: Similarly, purified RNF41 was able to mediate ubiquitination of Clec9A in vitro (Figure 4C).
evidence: Experimental data from in vitro ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 4C

claim: Several ubiquitination sites within the ectodomain of mClec9A were identified including K88 in the stalk region, and K167, K178, K195, K238, K246, K251, K257 and K258 within the CTLD.
source: This analysis revealed several ubiquitination sites within the ectodomain of mClec9A including K88 in the stalk region, and K167, K178, K195, K238, K246, K251, K257 and K258 within the CTLD (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), most of which are conserved in mouse and human Clec9A.
evidence: Experimental data from mass spectrometry shown in figures

claim: An increase in abundance of ubiquitinated Clec9A peptides was observed in the presence of RNF41, but not RNF41-ΔRING.
source: In addition, we observed an increase in abundance of ubiquitinated Clec9A peptides in the presence of RNF41, but not RNF41-ΔRING (Figure 4E, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Experimental data from mass spectrometry shown in figures

claim: RNF41 ubiquitinates the Clec9A ectodomain.
source: These results confirm that RNF41 ubiquitinates the Clec9A ectodomain, and that the RNF41 RING domain is essential for ubiquitination.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing ubiquitination sites in ectodomain

claim: The RNF41 RING domain is essential for ubiquitination of Clec9A.
source: These results confirm that RNF41 ubiquitinates the Clec9A ectodomain, and that the RNF41 RING domain is essential for ubiquitination.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing no ubiquitination with RING deletion

claim: K-48 linkages were detected on ubiquitin associated with Clec9A.
source: Using a K-48 linkage-specific ubiquitin antibody, we detected K-48 linkages on ubiquitin associated with Clec9A suggesting that Clec9A poly-ubiquitination could be mediated, at least in part, via K48-linkages (Figure 4A).
